outcome.answer:
Yes—recent papers directly link transformer-based recommenders to popularity bias, and some show scaling can make it worse. In transformer-based sequential recommenders, increasing model size improves accuracy but also amplifies popularity bias, over-recommending popular items and hurting niche items; one paper attributes this to spectral collapse caused by attention aggregation and feed-forward projections, and proposes SPRINT to improve both accuracy and long-tail fairness during scaling [1]. Another transformer-based sequential model, BT-SR, reports better long-tail item coverage and recommendation calibration while improving next-item prediction accuracy [8].

Several mitigation approaches differ in where they intervene. PR-entmax changes only the training loss, making popularity correction context-dependent and reducing popularity bias without architectural changes [3]. PopSteer is a post-hoc method for sequential recommendation that identifies neurons encoding popularity signals and steers them to improve fairness with minimal accuracy impact [6]. More broadly, popularity bias is also studied alongside other biases such as positivity bias, which can further amplify exposure unfairness toward popular items [2].
